title: Where Is It? Location, Geocoding and Privacy
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (paragraph for paragraph, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, acceptance criteria AC-1 to AC-3, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the location-and-geo entry in journal-spec.json. Units added by this conversion: a lead paragraph for the Trade-offs section (p51) and a synthesis paragraph (p63) before the hand-off in the closing section; the introduction's third paragraph gained the roadmap.

know: Country-shaped addresses, geocoding outputs, gazetteers and place hierarchies, precision levels and geo indexes.
The three representations per listing (restricted precise point, public point, place IDs) and the semantics of radius, polygon and place searches.
believe: Location is a small subsystem, not a field, and geocoding is a licensing decision before it is a technical one.
can_do: Find where their platform leaks a private seller's location, including through distances and API payloads.
Check whether their stored coordinates are licensed for storage, and why their filters, maps and landing pages disagree.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a location leak that the listing page did not show, the reader explains how it happened and what the model changes.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace shows only a postcode district on private sellers' listings, yet a buyer turned up at a seller's door. Using only this chapter: how could that happen, and what does the location model change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The precise point (a postcode centroid) was returned in an API payload and used for distances shown to one decimal, so a payload read or three searches located the door. Store a restricted precise point, derive a public point deterministically by precision policy, and compute every shown distance, map pin, feed and payload from the public point only, enforced on the server and checked by a weekly exposure scan with a target of zero.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Veldmark's five answers to 'where is it?'; what location means: kinds, addresses, geocoding, gazetteers, precision, geo indexes; three representations and their services, the public point and the rule for distances; radius, polygon and place semantics; geocoding providers and licences; the Rotterdam bike, the Lyon apartment, the Barcelona ring and quality metrics; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and the Chief Architect's view. Evidence: provider terms, standards and documentation, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: How do you model and process location so search, maps, trust and analytics work across countries?
thesis.claim: A listing's location is a small subsystem, not a field: it stores a restricted precise point, a public point derived from it deterministically by a group precision policy, and stable place IDs from a versioned gazetteer, so radius search, landing pages, duplicate detection, fraud signals and analytics each read the representation meant for them; distances, map pins, payloads, feeds and structured data are computed from the public point only, enforced on the server; and geocoder licence terms are recorded with every coordinate, because storage rights depend on provider, country and use.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that location is one coordinate field, geocoded once and read by every consumer, with privacy handled by what the listing page displays and geocoder choice a matter of price and accuracy.
thesis.so_what: A group that accepts this runs one gazetteer and geocoding gateway (Veldmark Place, approved in May 2027), makes the precision policy group policy with brand parameters, chooses providers per country and use behind the gateway and reviews their licences in every acquisition, and publishes location quality weekly, with a precise-point exposure target of zero and any exposure treated as a privacy incident.
thesis.how_why: Tradeyard showed '3014 Rotterdam' on the page but returned the seller's postcode centroid to six decimals in its search API and showed distances to one decimal, so a stranger found a seller's door; Hearthly Spain showed exact pins for private landlords. Search radius, landing pages, duplicate detection and fraud each need a different representation: the Barcelona ring's 35%-below-market signal exists only because rent medians are computed per small H3 cell.

supporting_claims.claim: A listing's location is a small subsystem, not a field: it has several kinds, country-shaped addresses, geocoder results that carry match level, confidence and provenance, a gazetteer of administrative and marketplace places, a precision scale and geo indexes for different jobs.

Location is stored as three representations, a restricted precise point, a public point derived from it deterministically by policy, and place IDs with all ancestors from a versioned gazetteer, each read by the consumers meant for it.

Privacy is enforced on the server: every distance, pin, payload, event, feed and structured-data field a buyer or partner can read is computed from the public point, and internal reads of the precise point are purposeful and logged.
Radius, place and polygon queries agree only when each reads a declared representation (a curated search origin, stored place IDs, public points) from one gazetteer shared across countries.
Geocoding is a licensing decision before it is a technical one: providers are chosen per country and per use, and the licence terms are recorded with every stored coordinate.
At group scale location needs one owner: one gazetteer and geocoding gateway, a group precision policy with brand parameters, providers behind the gateway, and published quality metrics.

role.contribution: Models location as three representations under a precision policy and a governed gazetteer, which search, maps, alerts, duplicate detection and fraud later read.

additional_patterns.applies_to: practice: the model tested on three Veldmark cases and quality metrics

flow.rationale: Each section supplies what the next needs. The scene poses the problem; the concepts give the vocabulary; the licences say what the geocoder outputs just defined may be stored and shown, which the architecture's gateway and provenance then rely on; the architecture combines concepts and constraints into three representations and the distance rule; query semantics are decisions about those representations; the Veldmark cases run the whole model; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's decisions and review questions are judgements about a model the reader has now seen. Moving the architecture before the concepts would use match levels, places and precision levels before they are defined, and moving the licences after it would describe a licence-aware gateway before the licences.

hook.content: A buyer searching 'within 10 km of Utrecht' gets a bike 14 km away; 'apartments in Lyon' leaves out Villeurbanne; a private seller's home can be worked out from distances in the app.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Five Answers to "Where Is It?"
sections.controlling_idea: A privacy complaint at Tradeyard and an inventory of five brand answers show that one location field read by every consumer leaks private locations, leaves licences unknown and blocks group search.

advances_thesis.how: Poses the problem the three representations and the server-side rule solve.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's plan, starting with Veldmark's five answers.
transition_in.introduces: The complaint that started Ingrid's review.

flow.rationale: One concrete leak first, then its mechanism, then the five brands' answers, then what those answers prevent at group level; the inventory reads as a diagnosis only after the reader has seen how one of its rows let a stranger find a door.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A Tradeyard seller in Rotterdam found a stranger at her door although the listing page showed only '3014 Rotterdam'.

evidence.what: Lucía Ortega brings Ingrid Halvorsen the complaint in late March 2027; the page showed only the postcode district.
evidence.shows: Sets a puzzle the page alone cannot explain.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The leak came from the system behind the page: distances computed from the full six-character postcode centroid and that centroid returned to six decimals in the search API, so a payload read or three searches located the door.

evidence.what: Distances to one decimal ('2.3 km') from the centroid of a six-character postcode; the centroid in the JSON payload to six decimal places.
evidence.shows: The page blurred the location but the API and the distances did not.

evidence.what: Figure 1: three distance circles intersect at the seller's front door.
evidence.shows: Shows trilateration from rounded distances.

transition_in.carries_over: The puzzle of how he found her.
transition_in.introduces: The reconstruction by Daan Visser's team.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each Veldmark brand captures, stores, shows and geocodes location differently, including exact pins for private landlords at Hearthly Spain.

evidence.what: Five rows: Tradeyard NL/BE, Tradeyard PL/PT, Motorvane, Hearthly FR, Hearthly ES, by capture, storage, public display and geocoder.
evidence.shows: The problem is not one brand's bug but five unrelated models.

transition_in.introduces: How every brand handles location.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each answer was reasonable alone, but together they leave Veldmark unable to say what location data it publishes about private individuals, whether its coordinates were licensed for storage, or to run one map, one cross-border search or one rent comparison.

transition_in.introduces: What they cost the group, and the model the rest of the chapter proposes.

sections.heading: Concepts: What "Location" Means for a Listing
sections.controlling_idea: Location is a subsystem of distinct concepts: kinds of location, country-shaped addresses, geocoder outputs, gazetteers and place hierarchies, a precision scale and geo indexes.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the parts the subsystem is made of.

transition_in.carries_over: Five inconsistent answers and the model Ingrid's team proposes.
transition_in.introduces: The vocabulary that model is built from.

flow.rationale: Kinds of location first (what is being located), then the address as captured, then geocoding that turns it into coordinates with a match level, then the places those coordinates fall in, then precision (which needs places to name its levels), then geo indexes that query all of it. Precision before places would leave its levels undefined; indexes first would index something not yet described.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A listing can carry four kinds of location, item, seller, handover and service area, and confusing them is the first modeling mistake; a kind says what is located, while how precisely one location is stored and shown is a separate question that the precision levels and the architecture answer.

evidence.what: Kind, definition, example, who needs it, for the four kinds.
evidence.shows: Each kind has different consumers, so one field cannot serve them all.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For goods, item and seller location usually coincide, which is why systems store one field, but they part often enough to matter, and shipping turns item location from a hard filter into a delivery-cost input.

evidence.what: A dealer group with ten branches, an item at a parent's house, a property listed by an agency elsewhere, shipped items; Tradeyard Safe Deal parcels.
evidence.shows: Shows when the single field breaks.

transition_in.introduces: Why systems usually store one, and when that breaks.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: There is no universal address model: postcodes alone differ in shape and meaning across Veldmark's countries, so address formats must be data per country.

evidence.what: Postcode shapes and specificity for NL, BE, DE/AT, FR, ES/PT/PL with consequences.
evidence.shows: Postcodes cross municipal borders, cover several communes or a street segment, so code cannot hard-wire one shape.

transition_in.introduces: How its address is captured.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Industry practice parses free-text addresses into components before matching, and libpostal does it well enough but heavily enough to run as a shared service.

evidence.what: libpostal: 99.45% full-parse accuracy on held-out data, '60+ languages', model about 1.8 GB.
evidence.shows: Parsing is solved well enough to rely on, and its size makes it a shared service.

transition_in.introduces: How free text becomes components.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Geocoding and reverse geocoding are inexact, so every geocoder result must keep its match level, confidence and provenance, and the licence makes provenance mandatory for location.

transition_in.introduces: Turning them into coordinates, and what to keep with the result.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A gazetteer is a reference dataset of named places with stable IDs, names, geometries and parent relations, and OpenStreetMap's admin levels and Who's On First show the design space.

evidence.what: OSM admin_level 2 to 10, meanings varying by country (Berlin at 4); Who's On First stable 64-bit IDs, multiple hierarchies, query by ID not name.
evidence.shows: Admin levels cannot serve as a cross-country hierarchy without mapping; stable IDs and multiple parents are possible.
evidence.source: OpenStreetMap Wiki n.d.; Who's On First n.d.

transition_in.introduces: The places they fall in.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Marketplaces need places with several parents and places no administration defines, so the gazetteer holds administrative places and curated marketplace places.

evidence.what: Lyon 7e in the commune, the Métropole and the Rhône; 'Randstad', 'Costa del Sol', 'Eixample'.
evidence.shows: Shows why one administrative tree is not enough.

transition_in.introduces: What a marketplace needs from them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Listings reference places by ID and carry all ancestor IDs, so 'all listings in Rotterdam' is a term filter and renaming a place changes no listing.

transition_in.carries_over: A gazetteer of administrative and marketplace places.
transition_in.introduces: How listings point at it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Location precision is the level of detail at which a location is known, stored or shown, and Veldmark adopts a six-level scale from P0 country to P5 exact.

evidence.what: P0 to P5 with Tradeyard NL and Hearthly FR examples.
evidence.shows: Gives policies a shared vocabulary across countries.

transition_in.introduces: Levels of detail named after them, completed by two finer levels (street and exact address).

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Precision applies three times, capture, stored and display, and the Rotterdam mistake was letting display precision follow stored precision with only the page template blurring it.

transition_in.introduces: The three moments they apply to, and the Rotterdam case read in those terms.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A geo index makes spatial queries cheap, and four families matter in listing systems: engine-native types, geohash, H3 and S2.

evidence.what: Elastic BKD trees and tessellation; geohash cell-edge problem; H3 (Uber 2018) 16 resolutions, 36.13 km² at res 6 to 0.105 km² at res 9; S2 levels 0 to 30, Hilbert ordering; Airbnb 2026 uses S2 cells as a feature.
evidence.shows: Each family has a different strength.
evidence.source: Elastic n.d.; Uber 2018; H3 docs n.d.; S2 n.d.; Airbnb 2026

transition_in.introduces: The data structures that query them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The four index families are complementary: engine-native types serve queries, H3 serves aggregation and privacy, and S2 or geohash serve key-value lookups.

transition_in.introduces: The job each one serves, with a pointer to the trade-offs.

sections.heading: Geocoding Providers and Licences
sections.controlling_idea: Geocoding and map-data licences decide what a marketplace may store, so providers are chosen per country and use, the licence is recorded with every coordinate, and most groups end up with a mix whose volumes are smaller than feared.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the terms that make geocoding a licensing decision and the rule that follows.

transition_in.carries_over: The concepts, including geocoder results that record provider and licence.
transition_in.introduces: The constraint to know before designing: what the providers' licences allow a marketplace to store and show.

flow.rationale: The terms first, as dated evidence; then the rule they force; then the build-versus-buy mix that follows; then the cost reassurance. The rule before the terms would ask the reader to accept a constraint without seeing it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Geocoding and map-data licences differ in ways that decide what a marketplace can store, as the providers' terms in October 2026 show, so the constraint must be known before the design.

evidence.what: Google (storage restricted, place IDs storable, display on a Google Map), Mapbox (temporary not cacheable, permanent=true paid), Nominatim public (1 request/second, no bulk), OSM data (ODbL share-alike), Pelias (MIT), national registers (BAG public domain mark, BAN Licence Ouverte 2.0, OS Open UPRN about 40 million locations).
evidence.shows: Storage, display and share-alike rights vary by provider, with consequences for a listing database.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The provider is chosen per country and per use, and the licence is a property of every stored coordinate, because storage, autocomplete and base maps are different uses with different terms.

transition_in.introduces: The rule they force.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Most groups end up with a mix: self-hosted national registers where open, a commercial geocoder with storage rights elsewhere, and an open-data gazetteer extended with curated places.

transition_in.introduces: The mix that results.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The volumes that drive geocoding cost are smaller than feared, because most private listings are geocoded from a postcode lookup and full-address geocoding is concentrated in feeds whose results can be stored.

transition_in.introduces: What it costs.

sections.heading: Architecture: Three Representations and the Services Behind Them
sections.controlling_idea: The location value object has three parts read by different consumers, produced by six components, with the public point derived deterministically and every buyer-facing distance, event and search field computed from the public side.

advances_thesis.how: Sets out the three representations and the server-side rule that keeps the precise point private.

transition_in.carries_over: The concepts and the licence constraints.
transition_in.introduces: The model assembled from them: one value object and the services behind it.

additional_patterns.applies_to: p27-p31: the distance rule, the internal exception and the event and search document that carry it out

flow.rationale: The value object first, because every later paragraph refers to its three parts, followed directly by how the parts derive from each other in the table's order; then the components that produce the parts, with Figure 2 after the list that numbers them, and the reason the precise part's store is restricted (personal data) right after the restricted store it explains; then the one derivation that decides privacy (the public point), closed by Airbnb's documented example of the same separation; then the rule for distances that depends on it; then the event and search document that carry the result downstream. Starting with the search document would show fields before the reader knows which part they come from; placing the personal-data evidence between the table and the derivation interrupted the table's line of thought.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: With the concepts and licence constraints in place, location inside the listing aggregate is a value object with three parts, precise location, public location and place references, written together but read by different consumers.

evidence.what: Part, contents, classification, readers for the three parts.
evidence.shows: Each part has its own classification and readers; clients and partners never read the precise part.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The table's order is also the order of derivation: each part can be recomputed from the one above it, which makes policy changes and boundary reforms backfills rather than migrations.

transition_in.carries_over: The three parts in the table's order.
transition_in.introduces: The table's order as the order of derivation, which makes changes backfills.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Six components produce and guard the three parts: country address capture, a geocoding gateway, a gazetteer service, a place resolver, a precision policy engine and a restricted location store.

evidence.what: Figure 2: location enters as text and leaves as two products; everything right of the policy engine sees only what the policy allows.
evidence.shows: Shows the flow through the components and the audited path to the restricted store.

transition_in.carries_over: The value object and how its parts derive from each other.
transition_in.introduces: The services behind it, with Figure 2 after the list that numbers them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The store is restricted because a private seller's precise location is personal data while the gazetteer is not, which the GDPR states and which the author's generic Productscape reference models show is easy to get wrong.

evidence.what: GDPR Art. 4(1): location data as one of the identifiers that make a person identifiable.
evidence.shows: The precise part carries a legal classification the other parts do not.

evidence.what: The author's two generic reference models built with Productscape, a product-domain modeling method introduced in business-capabilities, describing no real company: the real-estate model classifies geo reference data as non-personal and listings with a private owner's location as 'possible-personal'; the general-listings model's own review notes its non-personal classification is wrong for private sellers.
evidence.shows: Even reference models get the classification wrong for private sellers.

transition_in.carries_over: The restricted location store (component 6) and Figure 2's audited path.
transition_in.introduces: Why the precise part is restricted: it is personal data for private sellers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The precision policy can derive the public point by snapping to an H3 cell centre or by a seeded offset, and the offset must be deterministic or repeated versions average back to the true point.

evidence.what: H3 res 7 average edge 1.41 km, res 8 0.53 km.
evidence.shows: Gives the scale of a snapped public point.

evidence.what: Figure 3: seeded offset versus redrawn pins that average back to the house.
evidence.shows: Shows why determinism is required.

transition_in.introduces: How it derives the public point.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Both methods need two refinements: the public point must stay inside the public place, and in sparse areas the policy coarsens until the area holds a minimum number of addresses.

transition_in.introduces: Refinements that apply to both.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Airbnb's documented obfuscation shows the principle that the exact address is released for a reason, to a known person, not at publication.

evidence.what: 'within about a half mile (less than 1 kilometer) of the street address'; 'guests don't receive the address until their reservation is confirmed'.
evidence.shows: A large public platform separates public and precise location in the same way.

transition_in.introduces: A documented public example.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Distances shown to buyers and distance sorting must be computed from the public point and rounded to its precision, because precise distances turn three searches into a location.

transition_in.introduces: The rule for every distance a buyer sees, back to the Rotterdam case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Internal consumers such as duplicate detection and fraud models need the precise point, and read it from the restricted store with every read logged.

evidence.what: Figure 4: one precise point, many audiences.
evidence.shows: Shows public consumers on the derived side and internal models with a documented purpose on the precise side.

transition_in.carries_over: Buyer-facing distances from the public point.
transition_in.introduces: Internal consumers that need the precise one.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The listing event carries the public part and the place references, not the precise part, so the event stream and every downstream copy stay free of precise private locations.

evidence.what: Femke's bike listing existed in seven copies.
evidence.shows: Erasing a precise point from seven copies is harder than never writing it there.

transition_in.introduces: How the parts travel downstream in events.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The search document holds the public point, all place IDs and ancestors, H3 cell IDs and the display label and level.

transition_in.introduces: The search document built from it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For real estate the search document may also hold a precise point that is never returned and is used for polygon queries only where the agency chose exact display, and map-search owns the query design.

transition_in.introduces: The real-estate exception and the pointer to map search.

sections.heading: Radius, Polygon and Place: Getting the Semantics Right
sections.controlling_idea: Each kind of location query hides a decision, and the model makes each one explicit: a curated search origin, administrative and marketplace places, names on IDs, place filters on stored IDs and polygons on public points, one model across borders, and the routing provider's terms as a constraint.

advances_thesis.how: Shows that filters, maps and landing pages agree only when each query reads a declared representation.

transition_in.carries_over: The three representations and what the search document holds.
transition_in.introduces: The decisions hidden in the queries that read them.

flow.rationale: One query type per paragraph, from the simplest (radius origin) to the widest in scope (cross-border), with travel time last because it moves beyond the location model to a provider constraint and echoes the licences section. The place-versus-polygon rule needs the administrative and marketplace places and the names-on-IDs rule before it; placed earlier, it would use place IDs whose meaning had not been settled for the buyer's words.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each kind of location query hides a decision that becomes a visible bug if left implicit.
A radius needs an origin, and Veldmark's gazetteer stores a curated reference point for every place used as a search origin.

evidence.what: Rotterdam's municipality includes Hoek van Holland about 30 km from the centre, so its geometric centroid can fall somewhere unhelpful.
evidence.shows: A centroid is not always a sensible origin.

transition_in.introduces: The first: where a radius starts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: 'In Lyon' can mean the commune, the metropolis or a buyer's mental map, so the gazetteer offers an administrative and a marketplace place and query understanding chooses.

evidence.what: Villeurbanne, a separate commune inside the Métropole de Lyon.
evidence.shows: A single silent choice leaves out flats buyers expect.

evidence.what: Figure 5: commune outline, neighbouring commune, dashed marketplace place.
evidence.shows: Shows the two kinds of place side by side.

transition_in.introduces: What a place name means.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Names belong to place IDs, with aliases, so bilingual and alternative names resolve to one place.

evidence.what: Brussels-Capital Region's 19 municipalities with French and Dutch names; 'Elsene' and 'Ixelles'; 'The Hague', 'Den Haag', ''s-Gravenhage'.
evidence.shows: One place can have several names.

transition_in.introduces: Several names for one place.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Place filters use stored place IDs and polygons use public points, with the real-estate exact-display case as the one exception, and the listing page names the stored place, so what the buyer sees matches the filter that found it.

transition_in.introduces: Polygons and places, which can disagree at boundaries.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A cross-border radius is possible only with one coordinate system, gazetteer and index across countries, so a country fork rules it out before anyone decides whether it is wanted.

evidence.what: Motorvane in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland and Austria; a buyer in Aachen searching within 50 km covers parts of three countries.
evidence.shows: Cross-border search is a real product question the model can foreclose.

transition_in.introduces: Queries that cross a border.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Travel-time search shows that the routing provider's commercial model is an architectural constraint like the geocoder's licence.

evidence.what: Rightmove's 'My Places' uses the TravelTime API; the vendor case study says Rightmove chose a fixed annual licence with unlimited requests to avoid pay-as-you-go cost growth.
evidence.shows: Commercial terms shaped the design.

transition_in.introduces: Commute time, and the provider terms behind it.

sections.heading: In Practice at Veldmark
sections.controlling_idea: Three Veldmark cases and a weekly quality report show the model at work: the Rotterdam bike's public point reveals no more than a district, the Lyon apartment's agencies' choices are honoured consistently, the Barcelona ring is caught partly through location signals, and quality is measured.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the representations, the distance rule and the published metrics to fictional cases.

transition_in.carries_over: The model, its providers and its query semantics.
transition_in.introduces: The model run end to end on Veldmark's three cases, starting with a private seller like the one in the scene.

additional_patterns.applies_to: the three cases, March, May and July 2027

flow.rationale: The private-seller case first because it answers the scene's complaint; the agency case adds place hierarchies, seller choice and duplicates; the fraud case adds location as a trust signal; the quality metrics close because they measure everything the cases used. Putting the metrics first would measure a pipeline the reader has not seen run.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Femke, a different private seller in Rotterdam from the scene's complainant, listed her bike on the old model on 7 March; replayed under the policy adopted later in 2027, it is captured, geocoded, placed, given a P3 public point, indexed and searched in six steps, with a 2.6 km buyer seeing 'about 3 km'.

evidence.what: €240 city bike on Sunday 7 March 2027 at 19:42; postcode centroid; H3 res 7 public point inside 3014; 312 saved searches.
evidence.shows: Each step uses one representation and the distance rule.

evidence.what: ExifTool GPSLatitude and GPSLongitude tags.
evidence.shows: Photos carry coordinates the media pipeline must strip.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Nothing a buyer sees reveals more than the district: the precise centroid exists only in the restricted store, and a would-be visitor finds nothing more precise than a 5 km² cell.

evidence.what: Under the replayed model a would-be visitor finds nothing more precise than a 5 km² cell (H3 resolution 7).

sections.heading: The Chief Architect's View
sections.controlling_idea: Nobody owns location end to end, so at group scale it needs one owner and four explicit decisions, with signals to watch and a limit to where the design is worth it.

A decision before the gap would answer a problem not yet stated, and the policy before the gateway would put it in a service that does not yet exist.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In most organizations nobody owns location end to end, so at group scale it needs one owner and four explicit decisions.

conclusion.heading: From Place to Seller
conclusion.synthesis: The failures this chapter met had two causes. The first runs through all five answers in Ingrid's table: each brand stored one location and let every reader take what it needed, which let a stranger reach the Rotterdam door and left coordinates nobody could say were licensed. The second explains the opening's 'apartments in Lyon' landing page that left out Villeurbanne: there were no place references to choose between. One model removes both: three representations under a group policy, one gazetteer and a licence on every coordinate answer all three failures.
conclusion.so_what: The group fixes location once, as a shared service, instead of five brand fixes, and can then answer the regulator, the licensor and the cross-border buyer.

callback.to: The Rotterdam seller who found a stranger at her door, and the five answers to 'where is it?'.
callback.how: The reader can now say what the Rotterdam payload would carry under the model: a cell centre and a district, never a doorstep.

takeaway.content: Store three representations, compute everything public from the public point on the server, and record the licence with every coordinate.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The chapter's failures had two causes, one location read by every consumer (the leak and the unlicensed coordinates, in all five answers) and no place references (the opening's Villeurbanne gap); one model removes both, so the Rotterdam payload would carry a cell centre and a district, never a doorstep, and the group fixes location once as a shared service that answers the regulator, the licensor and the cross-border buyer.

Location says where a listing is, not who sells it, and even the precision rule depends on the seller's type and an agency's account settings, so the last subdomain the listing references, who lists, comes next.
